requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) For one day, keep a log in which you describe your communication activities. Keep track of the time and different ways you spend communicating, such as talking person-to-person, listening to teachers, listening to the radio or podcasts, watching television, using social media, reading books and other print media, and using any electronic communication device. Discuss with your counselor what your log reveals about the importance of communication in your life. Think of ways to improve your communication skills. (b) For three days, keep a journal of your listening experiences. Identify one example of each of the following, and discuss with your counselor when you have listened to each: obtain information, be persuaded, appreciate or enjoy something, and understand someone's feelings. (c) In a small-group setting, meet with other Scouts or with friends. Have them share personal stories about significant events in their lives that affected them in some way. Take note of how each Scout participates in the group discussion and how effectively each Scout communicates their story. Report what you have learned to your counselor about the differences you observed in effective communication. (d) List as many ways as you can think of to communicate with others (face-to-face, by telephone, letter, email, text messages, social media, and so on). For each type of communication, discuss with your counselor an instance when that method might not be appropriate or effective.

pamphlet_excerpts: Contact Person Phone: If you contact the person by phone, ask if this is a good timeto talk.
Not Time Ask: If it is not a good time, ask when you should callback.
Start Asking Person: Start by asking the person to spell his or her nameand tell you his or her title.
Speak Clearly Slowly: Speak clearly and slowly so the person can understand your questions. • If you do not understand a response, ask the same question inanother way.
step_by_step_procedure: State Response Ownwords: You could also state the response in your ownwords and ask if you got it right.
Follow-up Questions Todig: Use follow-up questions todig more deeply into a topic. • Save your hardest questions for last.
Conversationis Fresh Mind: While the conversationis still fresh in your mind, rewrite or type your notes foreasier reading.
Task Not Write: Your task is not to write down everything every personsays.

pamphlet_excerpts: Requirement Develop Plan: For requirement 6, you will develop a plan to teach a skill orinform someone about a subject.
Process Similar Prepare: Use a process similar to the one you used to prepare your shortspeech.
Form Outline Think: As you form the outline, think about how you couldbreak down the subject into step-by-step instructions.
Pick Asubject Skill: Pick asubject or skill that is (1) something you know well, and (2) something that a friend, relative, or troop member mightlike to learn.
step_by_step_procedure: Choose Basic Knots: First, choose four basic knots that are useful in differentsituations.
Foreach Knot Write: Foreach knot, write an outline that lists the steps for how to tiethe knot.
BSA Handbooks Resources: Look in the Scouts BSA handbooks, other Scouting resources, librarybooks, and search the internet (with your parent or guardian’spermission).
Want Enlarge Diagrams: You might want to enlarge these diagrams on aphotocopier or computer printer to make them easier for abeginner to follow.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Write to the editor of a magazine or your local newspaper to express your opinion or share information on any subject you choose. Send your message by fax, email, or regular mail. (b) Create a webpage or blog of special interest to you (for instance, your troop or crew, a hobby, or a sport). Include at least three articles or entries and one photograph or illustration, and one link to some other webpage or blog that would be helpful to someone who visits the webpage or blog you have created. Note: It is not necessary to post your webpage or blog to the internet, but if you decide to do so, you must first share it with your parent or guardian and counselor and get their permission. (c) Use desktop publishing to produce a newsletter, brochure, flyer, or other printed material for your troop or crew, class at school, or other group. Include at least one article and one photograph or illustration.
